[FACT] The user is currently working on a project.  
[EVENT] The user attended a 3-day project management workshop from March 15-17.  
[RELATIONSHIP] The trainer at the workshop was Rachel Brown.  
[PREFERENCE] The user is struggling to prioritize tasks.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant provided strategies to prioritize tasks effectively, including the MoSCoW Method, Eisenhower Matrix, Kano Model, and others.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The MoSCoW Method involves labeling tasks as Must-haves, Should-haves, Could-haves, and Won't-haves.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The Eisenhower Matrix categorizes tasks based on urgency and importance into four quadrants: Urgent & Important, Important but Not Urgent, Urgent but Not Important, and Not Urgent or Important.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant suggested breaking down large tasks into smaller chunks and using stakeholder input in the prioritization process.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant emphasized that prioritization is an ongoing process requiring continuous evaluation and adjustment.  
[USER] The user expressed interest in the MoSCoW method and the Eisenhower Matrix.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant provided detailed steps on how to implement the MoSCoW method in a real-world scenario, using a software development project for a banking institution as an example.  
[ASSISTANT_CREATED] The assistant created a task list for the MoSCoW method, including tasks like implementing login functionality, developing payment processing feature, and conducting security testing.

[USER] The user asked for advice on handling conflicting priorities from different stakeholders.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] The assistant recommended engaging with stakeholders to negotiate and find mutually acceptable solutions.
